http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/13/oil-s.text: Oil leaking from a tanker grounded off the coast of Oman is not only endangering a nearby island but has now also reached beaches on the Gulf Arab country’s mainland, to the north of the island, Oman’s environment authority said Wednesday.Crude oil has been leaking from the tanker Caroline Bezengi—a sanctioned tanker believed to be part of Russia’s “shadow fleet"—that was carrying nearly 1 million barrels of oil when it reported an explosion in June.No party has claimed responsibility for the incident, and the cause of the explosion has not been revealed.Oman, a sultanate on the southeastern coast of the Arabian Peninsula, has been a mediator in the ongoing war in Iran, which the United States and Israel launched on 28 February.Oil spill endangering marine protected areaEnvironmental experts said an oil spill has been spreading quickly in recent weeks from the partially submerged tanker off the shores of Qabiliyah Island, endangering a marine protected area there.According to recent satellite photos, the spill is rapidly spreading over an area of more than 600 square kilometres due to the monsoon season's strong winds and currents.The beaches of Ras Madrakah on mainland Oman, around 200 kilometres north of Qabiliyah Island, have also been contaminated, according to Oman's Environment Authority, which has been keeping an eye on the leak.The authorities also warned that the southern coasts of Masirah Island, over 300 kilometres north of the submerged tanker’s location, may also be affected in the coming hours.The 247-metre Caroline Bezengi, whose owners are thought to be situated in Shanghai, is believed to be part of Russia’s “shadow fleet” and has been sanctioned by the British government and the European Union for carrying Russian oil.It had left the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, in Russia, in May, according to geospatial data tracking company SynMax Maritime.

https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/08/17/volt.text: Menü Kereső A volt ukrán védelmi miniszter szerint néhány hónapon belül saját gyártású ballisztikus rakétákkal támadhatják Oroszországot Külföld Pál Tamás Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Ukrajna három-hat hónapon belül képes lehet arra, hogy saját gyártású ballisztikus rakétákkal csapást mérjen Oroszországra – mondta Mihajlo Fedorov volt ukrán védelmi miniszter a CBS Newsnak adott interjújában. Fedorov állítása szerint Ukrajna ballisztikusrakéta-programja az ő védelmi minisztersége idején gyorsult fel, és úgy véli, hogy Ukrajna még az év vége előtt ballisztikus rakétákat indíthat Oroszország területére. „Minden technológiai ciklusban le kell győznünk Oroszországot, és a nap 24 órájában, a hét minden napján döntéseket kell hoznunk” – mondta Fedorov, megjegyezve, hogy miközben Ukrajna gyors ütemben fejleszt és újít, Oroszország is ugyanezt teszi. Volodimir Zelenszkij ukrán elnök július közepén menesztette Fedorovot , azzal indokolva a döntést, hogy feloldhatatlan konfliktus alakult ki közte és Olekszandr Szirszkij főparancsnok között. A népszerű, 35 éves Fedorov leváltása országos, több ezer ember részvételével zajló tiltakozáshullámot indított el Ukrajnában . A fokozódó nyomás miatt az ukrán elnök Szirszkijt is leváltotta, új főparancsnoknak pedig a Fedorovhoz hasonló szemléletű Mihajlo Drapatijt nevezte ki. Fedorov miniszteri székét Jevhen Hmara, az Ukrán Nemzetbiztonsági Szolgálat (SZBU) ideiglenes vezetője kapta meg, de csak átmeneti időre. Arra a kérdésre, hogy szerinte miért menesztették, Fedorov azt mondta: „Tényleg nem akarok az amerikai közönségnek arról beszélni, hogy miért.” Hozzátette: „Bármi is legyen az ok, fontos megérteni, hogy Ukrajna folytatni fogja a harcot.” Fedorov azt mondta a CBS Newsnak, hogy a leváltása miatt kirobbant tiltakozások azt jelzik, hogy az ukrán emberek támogatják a demokratikus értékeket, és hogy Ukrajna a szabadságáért harcol. Azt nem árulta el, hogy tervezi-e a visszatérést a kormányzatba. „Hamarosan meglátjuk” – mondta. „De bármi is történjen, minden munkám arra fog irányulni, hogy véget vessünk a háborúnak és újjáépítsük Ukrajnát.” Az 1991-es születésű Fedorov 2019-ben Zelenszkij elnökválasztási kampányának digitális felelőse volt, majd az új kormány legfiatalabb tagjaként azonnal kormányfőhelyettes lett, és megkapta a digitális átalakításért felelős minisztérium vezetését is. Négy évvel később oktatási, tudományos és technológiai fejlesztésért felelős miniszter lett, majd két évvel később visszatért a digitális tárca élére, ahonnan 2026 elején a védelmi miniszter székébe ült át. Fedorov védelmi miniszteri kinevezése után a drónokra, a csúcstechnológiás hadviselésre és a beszerzésekre összpontosított. Az elmúlt hónapokban az ukrán hadsereg érezhetően növelte ütőképességét a drónipar látványos felfutásával, így gyakoribbá váltak az orosz területen végrehajtott mélységi ellencsapások is, amit nagyrészt Fedorov javára írtak. Starting December 17, 2026, LOT Polish Airlines will launch a weekly charter flight connecting Katowice International Airport in southern Poland directly to Puerto Vallarta. Operating every Thursday through March 18, 2027, the route uses a Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner with capacity for around 300 passengers, bringing roughly 1,200 Polish visitors to the Banderas Bay region each month. To lay the groundwork for the new route, the Puerto Vallarta Tourism Trust teamed up with tour operator Rainbow Tours for an intensive promotional roadshow across Poland. Travel representatives visited Katowice, Wroclaw, and Lódz, leading five detailed training seminars for 630 local travel advisors. Because Puerto Vallarta remains a relatively undiscovered destination for many Polish vacationers, these sessions gave agents the product knowledge and confidence needed to pitch the coastal destination to clients booking their winter getaways. Hotel partners joined the promotional tour to showcase the city’s diverse lodging scene, including representatives from Buenaventura Grand, Hacienda Buenaventura, Krystal Puerto Vallarta, Krystal Grand, and The Hacienda at Krystal Grand. Together, they highlighted package deals that bundle round-trip airfare, ground transfers, and seven-night stays with tailored local excursions. Beyond sunny beaches and an internationally acclaimed food scene, the vacation packages introduce visitors to the rich culture and many outdoor adventures in Puerto Vallarta. Travelers can book city cultural tours, seasonal whale-watching trips, or boat rides out to secluded spots like Majahuitas and Yelapa. For thrill-seekers, the Sierra Madre mountains offer off-road rides, zip-lining, and a chance to cross the Jorullo Bridge – the world’s longest vehicular suspension bridge. Packages also feature day trips into the heart of Jalisco’s heritage, with visits to the historic mountain town of San Sebastián del Oeste, the agave fields of Tequila, and the ancient circular pyramids of Guachimontones. This direct connection not only opens an accessible path for Polish tourists looking for winter relief, but it also marks a significant step forward in diversifying Puerto Vallarta’s European tourism market. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Donald Trump hosts China’s president, Xi Jinping, at the White House in September 2026. Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Donald Trump hosts China’s president, Xi Jinping, at the White House in September 2026. Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images Opinion Donald Trump Trump, Xi and Putin have a shared vision of global power – with no place for Europe Rafael Behr In a world carved into continental blocs by authoritarians, Britain has to make common cause with its neighbours Wed 18 Nov 2026 01.00 EST Last modified on Wed 18 Nov 2026 07.19 EST Share In the chronicles of 21st-century diplomacy few statements have caused as much offence with as few words as Barack Obama’s 2014 description of Russia as a “regional power” . Vladimir Putin’s politics were defined then, as now, by vengeful resentment of his country’s relegation from superpower status after the cold war. His worldview is warped by a paranoid conviction that Nato never stopped striving to deepen that humiliation, even after the USSR had unravelled. From his Kremlin throne, the Russian president expects to be treated as a colossus of world history. It is hard to overstate how bitterly he hated being dismissed by Obama as a geopolitical B-lister. In Donald Trump , Putin has a ready supplier of balm to soothe his injured vanity. The US president has a shallow, venal concept of power. He is impressed by gilded palaces and heavily armed thugs. He feels thwarted by American democracy and envies tyrants who operate without equivalent restraint. Since Trump measures greatness in a country by its leader’s contempt for smaller nations and appetite for self-enriching plunder, he willingly promotes Russia back to the top tier. That is the significance to Putin of a three-way summit with Trump and China’s Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Thursday. It confers trappings of parity with the world’s two genuine superpowers. That is a win for Russia, regardless of whether anything of substance is agreed. The agenda is vague. The Chinese foreign ministry has said the discussion will focus on “ safeguarding world peace ” and “promoting strategic stability in major-power relations”. Xi will be satisfied with the projection of China as convener of a new world order. Trump has said he expects the conversation to cover denuclearisation, Iran, trade and “my favourite subject, Ukraine”. The image of three leaders calibrating the balance of global power has been compared to Yalta, February 1945: Roosevelt, Stalin and Churchill drawing up plans for postwar Europe . That was a week-long conference where military allies were settling the fate of a defeated enemy. The analogy is revealing mostly as an expression of anxiety in those who will not be present. For many Europeans, Yalta conjures memories of cynical partition, with eastern nations condemned to decades of Soviet captivity. The fear in Kyiv is that Putin will use his privileged access to Trump’s ear to pour in poisonous theories about the origins of the Ukraine war and how to end it – a twisted narrative of Nato provocation, irresistible Russian superiority and the need for Europe to stop wasting money and US military hardware on a losing cause. The exclusion of European democracies from the room in Shenzhen is partly just a function of the conversation happening on the sidelines of a summit for countries with Pacific coasts. But it probes a deep strategic insecurity. Ukraine’s continental allies have asserted their rights to be part of any peace process but not found a way to turn that entitlement into a collective position, coordinated by a figure with diplomatic gravitas. After a round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi last week, Jared Kushner, one of Trump’s envoys, made the reassuring statement that a deal could not be done “without Europeans being at the table”. By contrast, Russia’s chief negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, accused the Europeans of lacking serious intent to find solutions. He dismissed their delegation to the Gulf as “tourists” who might as well “chat in the hotel bar”. That is standard Kremlin trolling, but it cuts with a shard of truth. It points to an old problem, often described with the apocryphal tale of Henry Kissinger complaining that there was no number to call when he wanted to speak to Europe. The challenge is more acute today. The institutional and economic foundations of European influence are under assault. Trump is ambivalent at best about Nato. His administration is protectionist and nationalist. Maga ideology casts liberal democratic Europe as a moribund civilisation erasing itself with mass immigration. China treats Europe as a bundle of consumers for manufactured exports whose politicians usually, by default, defer to Washington. The EU has ambitions of “strategic autonomy” but the process is slow and expensive. It means evolution from soft power – rivalling the US and China in economic heft as a single market whose regulations set global standards – to something a lot harder. European electorates may despise Trump and fear Putin, but they are not all comfortable with the choices that follow if the remedy is a shift in budget priorities to higher defence spending. A lot of European politics in recent years has been driven with a longing eye on the rear view mirror, wondering if there is a way back to the old world of open trade, respect for international law, a White House that wouldn’t abet the Kremlin in an imperial land grab. But there is growing recognition that Europe’s future cannot resemble its recent past. The UK is part of that story, and Andy Burnham has understood the implications. In a speech on Monday , the prime minister expanded his criticism of Brexit from the economic to the geopolitical arena. It was, he said, “the first domino to fall” in a pattern of global fragmentation. It introduced a schism in European alliances that was “exactly what our enemies wanted”. Burnham’s audit of the costs in forfeited trade was familiar enough, but he moved the argument up a gear by noting that withdrawal from the top table of European decision-making has cost Britain power and influence in the world. That is something continuity Brexiters cannot compute. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Matters of Opinion Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more after newsletter promotion As Burnham finds his pro-European voice, the old Eurosceptic myth-making industrial complex is grinding back into motion. Newspapers have published tenuous stories about the cost of restored alignment with Brussels and hypothetical migrant influxes. Veterans of the leave campaign are limbering up for a dismal dance around the 2016 totem pole. It is rotten from exposure to a decade of international storms. Britain is a regional power that undervalued the amplifying effect of EU membership. The benefits of being in the club felt enough like great-power status to fool Eurosceptics into thinking they could go it alone. They cling to that delusion. Kemi Badenoch has written about Britain having “latent great power attributes”. She doesn’t have a theory of how those dormant traits will be awoken in a world carved into continental blocs. Burnham’s plan is hardly precise, but at least he starts with facts: Britain is a European country; Europe will be safer and richer if it pools its resources; the UK should not want to be on the margin. A summit where Xi, Putin and Trump claim to be deciding the fate of the world may not yield much in the way of concrete deals, but it still contains a warning to European democracies. And a choice. One option is to boost leverage through closer continental cooperation. The alternative is flight into fantasies of immaculate national sovereignty and resurrected historical grandeur. One of those routes is a way for Europe to grow autonomy, security and prosperity in the 21st century. The other is the path of bitter self-defeat modelled by Brexit . Subscribe Heidi Alexander said bomb threats on flights across Europe were malicious hoax threats after at least 18 flights were reported affected on the same day. Passengers faced diversions, escorts and evacuations, and the cases described ended without explosives being found. - Advertisement - The disruption spread across Rome, Sofia, Prague, Madrid, Warsaw and Dublin-linked travel, making it the second time this week that flights across Europe were hit by similar threats. On Tuesday, at least seven flights were affected in the earlier wave. Rome, Sofia and Prague Authorities in Rome said they received an email threat from a group called Fighters of the Male State , which claimed to be targeting a feminist regime . An aircraft was escorted into Rome Fiumicino Airport by Italian Air Force jets, while the Bulgarian military said its jets escorted three aircraft to Sofia. In Prague, Czech police said no explosives were found aboard four flights after threats about an improvised explosive device . All four flights to Prague landed with no explosives found, and local media said the four flights had departed from Greece, Ireland and two from the UK. LOT Polish Airlines and Aer Lingus LOT Polish Airlines said two of its planes were affected, and one plane was stopped while taxiing and directed to a designated parking stand after reports of a potential security threat . LOT said no hazardous items were found and that passengers would continue their journey on a different aircraft. - Advertisement - Passengers and Aer Lingus flights also felt the disruption. One Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a French air base before passengers disembarked, while Spain's airport authority said bomb threats affected three flights at Madrid airport on Thursday and that the threat was ruled out after inspections. Europe's same-day security checks The pattern across Europe is unusually broad because the reports arrived on the same day and crossed multiple airports and airlines rather than staying inside one national system. That left airport teams, police and military units handling the immediate response in parallel, from diversion and escort procedures to checks on grounded aircraft. Heidi Alexander's description of the threats as hoaxes matches what the first wave of checks showed: authorities in several countries reported no explosives found in the incidents described. The unresolved issue is who sent the threats and whether the cases are connected, while investigators continue checking the flights and messages behind them.
